title: Code Signing
summary: Code signing is the use of a digital signature over a software artifact so that a consumer can verify who produced it and whether it has changed since it was signed. The signer hashes the artifact with a cryptographic digest and signs that digest with a private key; the verifier checks the signature with the corresponding public key, validates the certificate chain to a trusted root, and confirms the artifact digest matches. Signing is the mechanism behind operating system and package manager trust decisions, driver and installer approval, browser extension and mobile application distribution, container image trust policies and artifact repository promotion rules. For a practising engineer the interesting part is everything around the cryptography. Which identity signs, how that identity is proven to the certificate authority, where the private key lives, how the signing operation is authorised and logged, and how the trust decision is enforced at the point of installation or deployment all determine whether signing provides real assurance or merely ceremony. Weaknesses that keep recurring are long-lived unprotected private keys, signing services reachable from a compromised build job, verification that checks a signature exists but not whose it is, timestamping omitted so signatures expire with the certificate, and revocation infrastructure that is never consulted. Modern practice moves towards short-lived keys held in hardware or a managed signing service, keyless signing bound to a workload identity, transparency logs that record every signing event, and build provenance that binds an artifact to the exact source revision and build definition that produced it.
objectives: You will be able to explain the signing and verification flow, including certificate chain validation, digest comparison and the role of timestamping.
You will be able to describe how signing trust is consumed by operating systems, package managers, container runtimes and browsers.
You will be able to design a signing key custody model using hardware modules or managed signing services with authorised, logged use.
You will be able to identify common verification failures, such as accepting any valid signature regardless of signer identity or skipping revocation checks.
You will be able to explain build provenance and how it binds an artifact to its source revision and build definition.
You will be able to assess what a signing programme would and would not prevent if a build system were compromised.

beginner.definition: Code signing is the practice of adding a digital signature to a software file so people can check who made it and whether anyone changed it. Think of it as a tamper-evident seal on a package. Your device checks that seal before it trusts the file.
beginner.whyItMatters: Without signing, you cannot tell a real update from a fake one. An attacker could swap a download for malicious software that looks identical. Signing gives your operating system, browser, or package manager a way to say yes or no before running code. It protects millions of users from silent tampering, and it makes attackers work much harder.
howItWorks: The software maker creates a unique private key (a secret code only they hold).
They run a hash, a math function that turns the file into a short fingerprint.
The private key signs that fingerprint, and the signature is published with the file.
Your device rebuilds the fingerprint and checks it against the signed one.
It also checks the certificate chain, the linked proof that the signer is who they claim.
If all checks pass, the file is trusted and the software is allowed to run.
beginner.example: Imagine you order a medicine online. The bottle arrives with a sealed cap and a printed batch number. If the seal is broken, you do not take the medicine. Code signing works the same way. The seal is the signature, and the batch number is the fingerprint of the file. A pharmacy that checks the seal before selling protects you. Software that checks a signature before installing protects your computer the same way.
takeaways: A signature proves who built a file and that nobody changed it.
Always verify the signer identity, not just that a signature exists.
Keep signing keys in hardware or a managed service, never on a laptop.
